Why Gödel Waited for Turing

GÖDEL, Kurt.

Typed letter signed ‘Kurt Gödel’ to Martin Davis, with autograph postscript and manuscript emendations, on his 1934 Princeton lectures, Church’s Thesis, and his contributions to The Undecidable.

Princeton, New Jersey: The Institute for Advanced Study, 15 February 1965. $25,000

A typed letter signed by Kurt Gödel — widely held to be the greatest logician since Aristotle — written on the headed paper of the Institute for Advanced Study, corrected throughout in his own hand and closing with a one-line autograph postscript, addressed to the logician Martin Davis as Davis was seeing Gödel’s work through the press for his anthology The Undecidable (1965). In it Gödel sets down, more sharply than anywhere else in his published or unpublished writing, his refusal to let a footnote from his 1934 Princeton lectures be read as an anticipation of Church’s Thesis — the proposition, since called the Church–Turing thesis, that the intuitive notion of an effectively calculable function is captured exactly by a precise mathematical definition. The leaf is doubly annotated: Gödel’s emendations stand beside Davis’s own working marks in red ink and pencil, so that the sheet records both sides of the editorial exchange between the author of the incompleteness theorems and the mathematician who first put the 1934 lectures into print. It is the most substantive of the small group of letters Gödel wrote Davis in these years, and the one in which he states his reservations about the foundations of computability theory in his own words.

From February to May 1934 Gödel had lectured at the Institute on the undecidability results he had published in 1931. Stephen Kleene and J. Barkley Rosser, recruited by Oswald Veblen as note-takers, wrote the lectures down, and their text — ‘On Undecidable Propositions of Formal Mathematical Systems’ — was mimeographed in instalments to subscribers and a few libraries, then passed from hand to hand for three decades without formal publication. The change of title from the 1931 paper, ‘On Formally Undecidable Propositions of Principia Mathematica and Related Systems’, signals the wider ambition: where the earlier work had fixed on one formalism, the lectures defined a formal system in general, as a system of symbols with rules of inference and axiom-formation specified by finitary procedures, precisely to dispel the idea — still held by Church among others — that incompleteness might be an artefact of the particular system chosen. Gödel then defined the functions now called primitive recursive and noted that each can be computed, for any given arguments, by a finite procedure; aware, from the examples of Wilhelm Ackermann and Gabriel Sudan, that some computable functions outrun the primitive recursive ones, he introduced in the lectures’ final section the broader class of general recursive functions. To the remark about finite computation he attached his third footnote, conjecturing as a ‘heuristic principle’ that the converse holds if recursions of more general kinds are admitted — while insisting in the same breath that this could not be proved, because the notion of finite computation had not been defined. The qualification was not modesty but doctrine: Gödel did not yet believe that any formal definition of recursion exhausted what could be computed.

The results the lectures expounded were the two Gödel had proved in 1931 and that have governed mathematical logic ever since: that any consistent formal system rich enough to express arithmetic contains a true sentence it cannot prove, and that no such system can prove its own consistency from within. Together they ended David Hilbert’s programme of securing all of mathematics by a finitary consistency proof, and forced the recognition that truth and provability do not coincide. The 1934 lectures carried the argument further by framing it for formal systems as such, and by isolating, in the recursive functions, the precise notion of a step-by-step calculation on which both the incompleteness proof and the coming theory of computation would turn. It was at exactly this junction — where a theorem about the limits of proof became a question about the limits of mechanical calculation — that footnote 3 stood, and it is this junction the letter polices.

The conjecture mattered because of what Alonzo Church was proposing in Princeton at the same moment. In 1932–33 Church had set out a new system of logic in his two-part ‘A Set of Postulates for the Foundation of Logic’; though Kleene and Rosser proved the full system inconsistent in 1935, its computational core, the λ-calculus, survived, and with it Kleene’s results on the λ-definability of a wide range of effectively calculable functions. On the strength of those results Church advanced his Thesis: that every effectively calculable function is λ-definable, and hence that the informal idea of effective calculability coincides with a precise formal one. He put the proposal to Gödel in conversation early in 1934, undertaking to prove of any definition of effective calculability Gödel might offer that it was already included in λ-definability. Gödel was unpersuaded — Church reported to Kleene the following year that Gödel had thought the suggestion thoroughly unsatisfactory — because the identification rested on no direct analysis of the concept of a finite procedure, but only on the accident that several formalisms happened to agree. Here is the surprise the letter preserves: Gödel withheld assent from the thesis that now carries his collaborators’ names for the better part of a decade, and the letter explains, thirty years on, exactly why.

When Davis prepared the lectures for The Undecidable, the introduction he drafted treated footnote 3 as a statement of Church’s Thesis. Gödel’s reply is a point-by-point correction. He objects first to Davis’s claim that the lectures merely sought undecidability results for formal systems ‘in general’, pointing to the precise and widely applicable result of his sixth section, and noting that for languages with variables ranging over integers the most general result follows from his simply by dropping one condition. Then he reaches the heart of the matter: ‘it is not true that footnote 3 is a statement of Church’s Thesis’. The footnote, he explains, concerned only the equivalence of finite computation and recursive procedure; at the time of the lectures he was not convinced that his concept of recursion comprised all possible recursions, and the equivalence between his own definition and Kleene’s — published in Mathematische Annalen 112 (1936) — was, he notes, not quite trivial. He presses Davis to count among the lectures’ true novelties the transformation of the undecidable proposition into a problem about a Diophantine equation, and the abandonment of the cumbersome italicising scheme of the 1931 paper, and gently corrects Davis’s description of the new proof as ‘much simpler’ than its predecessor.

The letter then descends to the meticulous detail that was characteristic of Gödel’s dealings with his own texts. He lists the further corrections he had already made to the manuscript before sending it on to Professor Shepherdson and other publishers: a new footnote added to the sheet of insertions enclosed; the phrase ‘up to transformations by the arithmetical rules of computation’ inserted into footnote 17; the word ‘his’ inserted before a cross-reference in the extended footnote on Herbrand’s two definitions; and a series of small substitutions and deleted commas in the postscript, each specified by page and line. He turns at last to the English version of his 1931 paper, which he judges inferior to what he had expected and marred by an error he has found, and — surprised to have been given no part in the matter — asks whether the translation Jean van Heijenoort was preparing, published in 1967 in From Frege to Gödel, might be used in its place. The signature is followed by a one-line autograph postscript recording that the changes he had made to his Princeton Bicentennial lecture were merely stylistic.

Behind the technical caution lay a deeper one. Gödel’s reluctance to certify any single formalism as the definition of effective calculability sprang from a doubt that an epistemological notion of that kind could be given an absolute, system-independent definition at all — a doubt he had voiced at the Princeton Bicentennial Conference of 1946, the remarks for which are among the proof-sheets this letter returns. The general recursive functions he had defined in the lectures grew out of a suggestion of Jacques Herbrand, whose two definitions are the subject of one of the footnotes Gödel here corrects; through Kleene they became one of the standard formal accounts of computability, and one of the rival definitions of effective calculability that Church and Turing brought forward in 1936. What eventually struck Gödel was that this class turned out to be absolute — that the diagonal procedure, which in his hands had always led outward from a given system to a fresh undecidable sentence, did not lead outside the recursive functions. That a precise definition should so completely capture an intuitive epistemological notion he came to regard as a kind of miracle; it is the measure of his caution that in 1934 he had refused to take the mere coincidence of formalisms for the thing itself.

What finally moved Gödel was not Church’s λ-calculus nor his own recursive functions but Alan Turing’s analysis of mechanical procedure in ‘On Computable Numbers’ (1936–37). What set Turing’s account apart, in Gödel’s eyes, was that it did not posit a formalism and ask to be believed but argued from below: Turing analysed what a human computer actually does — reading and altering finitely many symbols, holding only a bounded amount in view at each step, moving by local rules — and derived his machine from those conditions, so that the definition came with its own justification rather than resting on the coincidence of independent definitions. Only after Turing had so reduced computation to the operations of an idealised machine did Gödel regard the informal notion of effective calculability as having been pinned down, and he said so in the postscript he composed for this very volume: that owing to Turing’s work a precise and unquestionably adequate definition of a formal system could at last be given, so that the question raised in footnote 3 could now be answered affirmatively. The point recurred in his later writing, where he treated Turing’s analysis of mechanical procedure, rather than the extensional agreement of the rival definitions, as the thing that carried conviction. Wilfried Sieg has since argued that this instinct was sound — that the often-cited ‘confluence’ of the Church, Gödel, Post and Turing definitions is weaker evidence for the thesis than is generally supposed, and that it is Turing’s conceptual argument that does the real work. The letter is the document in which Gödel himself draws that distinction, and dates his own assent to Turing rather than to Church.

The sheet carries the editorial transaction on both sides. On the first leaf, beside Gödel’s denial that footnote 3 states Church’s Thesis, Davis has looped the author’s margin-inserted sentence into its place in the argument; on the second, against Gödel’s numbered list of further changes, he has entered check-marks item by item and noted a page-reference in red, ‘Rf. P.78’, keying one of Gödel’s instructions to the proof-sheet it governs. The marks are in red ink and pencil, the working apparatus of an editor reconciling an author’s emendations against type already set. The letter is therefore not merely a statement of Gödel’s views but the surviving record of how those views entered the printed text of The Undecidable — the corrections proposed by the author and acknowledged, one by one, by the editor who carried them through to press. Its substance has long been part of the scholarly record: Kleene quoted the passage on footnote 3 in his note to the lectures in Gödel’s Collected Works, and both Feferman and John Dawson drew on the exchange in reconstructing Gödel’s slow road to the Church–Turing thesis. Few documents in the literature of computability show its two foundational figures at such close quarters over a single page.

Martin Davis (1928–2023), born in the Bronx and turned toward the theory of recursive functions by Emil Post during his student years at the City College of New York, had taken his Princeton doctorate in 1950 under Church and was, in 1965, professor at the Belfer Graduate School of Science at Yeshiva University, the address to which the letter is sent; he moved that year to the Courant Institute, where he spent the rest of his career. He is remembered for his part in the resolution of Hilbert’s tenth problem — his early conjecture that every listable set is Diophantine, carried forward with Hilary Putnam and Julia Robinson and completed by Yuri Matiyasevich in 1970 — and for the Davis–Putnam procedure at the root of modern satisfiability solving. The Undecidable gathered the founding papers of the subject by Gödel, Church, Turing, Kleene, Rosser and Post, each with Davis’s introductory note, and gave the 1934 lectures their first formal publication, thirty-one years after they were delivered. Davis himself translated two of Gödel’s German pieces — the colloquium notes Zur intuitionistischen Arithmetik und Zahlentheorie (1933) and Über die Länge von Beweisen (1936), whose proof-sheets this letter returns — while the 1931 paper appeared in Elliott Mendelson’s version, the translation Gödel here found wanting and asked to replace with van Heijenoort’s. For a generation of mathematicians and the first computer scientists the volume was the single accessible gathering of the field’s founding texts. Gödel’s scrupulous attention to the volume, recorded across this correspondence, is of a piece with his lifelong supervision of every reprint and translation of his work.

Gödel (1906–1978) was born in Brünn, took his doctorate at Vienna under Hans Hahn and proved the incompleteness theorems in 1931; he emigrated to the United States in 1940, fleeing the Nazi regime by way of the Trans-Siberian railway, and joined the Institute for Advanced Study, where Albert Einstein became one of his closest friends and where, taking emeritus standing in 1976, he worked until his death in 1978. His autograph is among the rarest of any modern mathematician of comparable stature: his papers passed to the Institute and were deposited at Princeton’s Firestone Library, where they remain in institutional hands under the Institute’s reserved copyright, so that only the letters he sent to independent correspondents can reach the market at all — and letters of genuine logical content, as against the notes of business and acquaintance that make up the great bulk of any correspondence, are rarer still. From the 1934 footnote that Gödel declined to call a statement of Church’s Thesis runs the whole settled apparatus of computability — recursive functions, the universal machine, the undecidability of the Entscheidungsproblem — the foundation of theoretical computer science and of the machines that were built upon it. This letter marks the one point at which its author paused over that identification, and named Turing as the reason he was at last willing to make it. That it also carries Davis’s answering marks gives it a second standing as evidence, for it preserves not only what Gödel thought but the manner in which his second thoughts reached print; among the autograph remains of the founders of computability, a letter of this content, in this condition of use, is of the first rank. Provenance: from the papers of Martin Davis, the letter’s recipient and the editor of The Undecidable.

Physical description

4to (280 × 218 mm), 2 pp. on two leaves of Institute for Advanced Study ‘School of Mathematics’ letterhead, typed in black and dated February 15, 1965, addressed to Professor Martin Davis at the Belfer Graduate School of Science, Yeshiva University, New York; signed in ink ‘Kurt Gödel’ at the foot of the second leaf, with a one-line autograph postscript beneath the signature in the same ink, and the typist’s notation ‘KG:RM’ with ‘Encl.’ at lower left. Manuscript emendations to the typescript in Gödel’s hand, including an inserted passage bracketed in ink in the left margin of the first leaf; further working marks in the hand of the recipient, Martin Davis, in red ink and pencil — check-marks, a deletion, and page references (‘Rf. P.78’) keyed to the proof-sheets under discussion. Stapled at the upper left corner, with light creasing and staple-related tears at that corner; otherwise clean and sound. A full transcription accompanies the letter.
